topics.summary: Oral/pharyngeal SCC; SCC of esophagus; hepatocellular carcinoma; breast cancer.

hySections.heading: Alcohol
bullets: Oral/pharyngeal SCC; SCC of esophagus; hepatocellular carcinoma; breast cancer.

hySections.heading: Aflatoxin
bullets: Answer on USMLE if they mention peanut farming in China.
Can cause hepatocellular carcinoma. On one offline Step 1 NBME.

hySections.heading: Aniline dyes
bullets: Answer on USMLE for hematuria in textile factory worker.
Can cause transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) of the bladder.
Aniline dyes are a type of industrial clothing dye.

hySections.heading: Arsenic
bullets: Answer on USMLE for Mees lines (white lines on nails), or palms + soles rash, in a gardener.
Arsenic is in many fertilizers; a small amount causes plants to flourish; poisoning seen in gardeners/landscapers, clearly.
An NBME Q gives pic of Mees lines in gardener → answer = arsenic.

hySections.heading: Asbestos
bullets: Asbestosis → lung disease (usually restrictive) with ferruginous bodies and supradiaphragmatic / pleural plaques.
NBME Q shows pic of ferruginous body and asks what cell initiates pulmonary fibrosis → answer = macrophage. (Ferruginous bodies in asbestosis)
The pleural / supradiaphragmatic plaques can be described simply as “soft tissue densities” seen on CXR.
Can develop into mesothelioma → can appear as white cancer that circumferentially envelops the lungs; NBME Q asks for “mesothelial cells” as the answer.
Shipyard workers, construction workers, and electricians are buzzy professions on USMLE for asbestosis.

hySections.heading: Benzene
bullets: Leukemias.

hySections.heading: Ethanol
bullets: Highest yield = esophageal squamous cell carcinoma + hepatocellular carcinoma.
Breast cancer carries theoretical association but USMLE doesn’t give a .

hySections.heading: 2-naphthylamine
bullets: Used to be used in some industrial dyes. Use discontinued to due carcinogen risk.
Causes collecting duct cancer (on NBME), and urothelial cancer in general.

hySections.heading: Nitrosamines
bullets: Gastric cancer.
Associated with consumption of smoked / cured meats.

hySections.heading: Processed meats
bullets: Colorectal cancer.

hySections.heading: Radon
bullets: Adenocarcinoma of the lung in non-smokers.
Due to background radiation from the ground; considered the second-most important cause of lung cancer after smoking.

hySections.heading: Smoking/tobacco
bullets: Basically every cancer.

hySections.heading: UV light
bullets: Skin cancer.

hySections.heading: Vinyl chloride
bullets: Hepatic angiosarcoma.
Can appear as nodular lesions of the liver (tricky, because can resemble metastases).

topics.summary: Fungus.

hySections.heading: Aspergillus
bullets: Fungus.
Can produce aflatoxin, which increases risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

hySections.heading: Clonorchis sinensis
bullets: Trematode (fluke); a type of helminth (parasitic worm).
Can cause cholangiocarcinoma (cancer of the bile ducts).
Treat with praziquantel.

hySections.heading: EBV
bullets: Ebstein-Barr virus is part of Herpesviridae (DNA; enveloped; ds-linear).
Causes nasopharyngeal carcinoma and B-cell lymphomas (Hodgkin and NHL).

hySections.heading: Helicobacter pylori
bullets: Spiral-shaped gram-negative rod.
Causes mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, a type of B-cell lymphoma.
I discuss H. pylori in detail in the HY Gastro PDF.

hySections.heading: HepB/C
bullets: Hepatocellular carcinoma

hySections.heading: HHV-8
bullets: Human herpesvirus 8 (aka Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus).
Kaposi sarcoma.

hySections.heading: HIV
bullets: Human immunodeficiency virus.
Primary CNS lymphoma at CD4 counts generally <100/µL.

Immunodeficiency in general can increase risk of squamous cell carcinomas (e.g., anal SCC in MSM; esophageal SCC in smoking/alcohol; SCC of skin due to sunlight); NBME Qs can occasionally mention immunodeficiency in Qs to imply SCC.

hySections.heading: HPV 16/18
bullets: Human papillomavirus.
Squamous cell carcinoma (usually genital/anal).

hySections.heading: Malignancy-associated microbes — High-Yield Pearls
bullets: Yes there are other strains, but chill. USMLE cares about 16/18, not the other ones you can run off.

hySections.heading: HTLV

Can cause cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) and T-cell leukemia (Sezary syndrome).

hySections.heading: Schistosoma hematobium

topics.title: autoantibodies
topics.summary: Anti-b2-microglobulin; anti-cardiolipin; lupus anticoagulant.

hySections.heading: Antiphospholipid syndrome
bullets: Anti-b2-microglobulin; anti-cardiolipin; lupus anticoagulant.
The latter is the name for either of the former two if the patient happens to have SLE.
Presents as in vivo thromboses despite an ↑ in vitro aPTT.
These antibodies are associated with recurrent miscarriage.
Can cause false-positive syphilis screening (i.e., SLE patient who gets positive syphilis VDRL test).

hySections.heading: Bullous pemphigoid
bullets: Anti-hemidesmosome (bullous pemphigoid antigen).
Hemidesmosomes connect the dermis to epidermis at the basement membrane.
In BP we see linear immunofluorescence on skin biopsy because hemidesmosomes line the basement membrane.
Q can say there are sub-epidermal blisters (pemphigus vulgaris, in contrast, the Q can say intra-epidermal blisters).
Usually no oral involvement, but not mandatory rule.
No Nikolsky sign (i.e., no sloughing of skin with friction).

hySections.heading: Pemphigus vulgaris
bullets: Anti-desmosome (anti-desmoglein 1 and 3).
Desmosomes connect adjacent epidermal cells side-to-side.
In PV we see a net-like immunofluorescence on skin biopsy because the desmosomes are between / outline the skin cells.
Q can say there are intra-epidermal blisters (bullous pemphigoid, in contrast, the Q can say sub-epidermal blisters).
Can present with oral involvement, albeit not mandatory.
(+) Nikolsky sign (i.e., sloughing of skin with friction).

hySections.heading: Goodpasture syndrome
bullets: Anti-collagen IV (anti-GBM; glomerular basement membrane).
Goodpasture presents as male 20s-40s with hematuria + hemoptysis + anti-collagen IV antibodies.
Causes linear immunofluorescence on renal biopsy, since collagen IV lines basement membranes.
Don’t confuse with Alport syndrome, which is XR disorder due to mutations in type IV collagen (not Ab).
Alport presents as male with red urine + eye/ear problem.

hySections.heading: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener)
bullets: c-ANCA, aka anti-proteinase 3 (anti-PR3).
Dumb mnemonic I created that helps some of my students: Water Closet (Wegener C-ANCA).
Presents are hematuria + hemoptysis + “head-itis” (i.e., problem with the head, e.g., nasal septal perforation, mastoiditis, sinusitis, necrotizing otitis).
Sometimes has neuro findings (mononeuritis multiplex).

hySections.heading: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss)
bullets: p-ANCA, aka anti-myeloperoxidase (anti-MPO).
Presents as asthma + eosinophilia.

hySections.heading: Microscopic polyangiitis
bullets: p-ANCA (anti-myeloperoxidase).
Presents as usually just red urine in person with (+) p-ANCA.

hySections.heading: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
bullets: Anti-double-stranded DNA (dsDNA).
Anti-Smith (ribonucleoprotein).
Anti-hematologic cell line Abs.
Lupus anticoagulant.
Should be noted that anti-dsDNA goes up in acute flares + best reflects renal prognosis.

hySections.heading: autoantibodies — High-Yield Pearls
bullets: Anti-Smith is more specific than anti-dsDNA, meaning it shows up less often than anti-dsDNA, but if it does show up, the patient absolutely is ruled-in for having SLE.
Thrombocytopenia is an exceedingly HY finding in SLE due to the anti-hematologic cell line Abs.

If all cell lines are down in SLE, aplastic anemia (i.e., ↓ bone marrow production) is wrong answer; choose “increased peripheral destruction” as answer instead, since the cause is merely antibodies against the cells.
Lupus anticoagulant I discussed above in anti-phospholipid syndrome; causes recurrent miscarriages and false (+) syphilis tests.

Most common presenting feature in SLE overall is arthritis. The Q need not mention malar rash (I’d say only ~1/3 of Qs). So if you get, e.g., 34-year-old woman with arthritis and thrombocytopenia + no other info, that is pass-level SLE till proven otherwise.
Complement protein C3 can be down in SLE flares.
Renal diagnosis for lupus nephritis is basically always diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (DPGN) on NBME.

Presents as pentad of 1) thrombocytopenia, 2) schistocytosis (the combo of 1+2 is called microangiopathic hemolytic anemia; MAHA), 3) renal issues (hematuria or ↑ RFTs), 4) fever, 5) neurologic signs.

hySections.heading: Drug-induced lupus (DIL)
bullets: Anti-histone antibodies.
Caused by various drugs (Mom is HIPP): Minocycline, Hydralazine, INH, Procainamide, Penicillamine.
Presents usually as arthritis + pericarditis or mediastinitis in patient who was given one of the above buzzy meds.

hySections.heading: Myasthenia gravis
bullets: Post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antibodies.
Sometimes a paraneoplastic of thymoma, but need not be.
Presents usually as 40s woman with triad of diplopia, eyelid ptosis, and dysphagia or hoarseness of voice. Gets worse with activity, whereas Lambert-Eaton improves.
USMLE wants pyridostigmine (cholinesterase inhibitor) as Tx.

hySections.heading: Lambert-Eaton
bullets: Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies.
Sometimes a paraneoplastic of small cell lung cancer.
Presents as proximal muscle weakness that improves with activity (e.g., patient can stand up from chair after trying a few times).

hySections.heading: Small cell cerebellar dysfunction
bullets: Anti-Hu/-Yo.
Presents as ataxia in someone with small cell lung cancer and negative CNS imaging (meaning metastases to brain aren’t the cause of the neurologic issues).

hySections.heading: Polymyositis / Dermatomyositis
bullets: Anti-Jo1.
Polymyositis and dermatomyositis are usually idiopathic autoimmune conditions, but they can sometimes be a paraneoplastic of ovarian cancer.
Present as proximal muscle weakness on physical examination + increased serum CK.
Dermatomyositis = polymyositis + skin findings. The latter are shawl rash, Gottron papules, mechanics hands, and heliotrope rash.

hySections.heading: Limited-type systemic sclerosis / scleroderma
bullets: Anti-centromere.
Scleroderma = another name for systemic sclerosis.
Limited type merely = CREST syndrome = Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias.
Pulmonary fibrosis leading to pulmonary HTN is HY for both limited and diffuse types of scleroderma.

hySections.heading: Diffuse-type systemic sclerosis / scleroderma
bullets: Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70).
Can present as same findings as in limited-type, but also with malignant HTN (e.g., BP of 220/120) due to renal involvement causing a surge of RAAS.

hySections.heading: Primary biliary cirrhosis
bullets: Anti-mitochondrial.
Presents as woman 20s-50s with ↑ ALP, direct bilirubin, and serum cholesterol, with generalized pruritis and Hx of other autoimmune disease in her or family member (e.g., RA, SLE).

hySections.heading: Autoimmune hepatitis
bullets: Anti-smooth muscle.
Presents as woman 20s-30s with idiopathic elevation of hepatic transaminases.
Diagnosis of exclusion (meaning you have to eliminate the other answer choices to get there).

hySections.heading: Rheumatoid arthritis
bullets: Rheumatoid factor (an IgM Ab against the Fc region of IgG).
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies.
Anti-CCP is more specific than rheumatoid factor for RA.

hySections.heading: Sjögren syndrome
bullets: Anti-SS-A (anti-Ro); anti-SS-B (anti-La).
Presents as xerostomia (dry mouth) + xerophthalmia (dry eyes) + arthritis.

hySections.heading: Graves disease
bullets: Anti-TSH receptor; this antibody is called thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin, or TSI, and activates the TSH receptor.
Most common cause of hyperthyroidism.
Exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema are HY findings.

hySections.heading: Hashimoto thyroiditis
bullets: Anti-thyroperoxidase, aka anti-microsomal antibodies.
Anti-thyroglobulin.
Highest yield cause of hypothyroidism in Western countries.

topics.summary: Mechanism

hySections.heading: Hypersensitivity types — High-Yield Pearls
bullets: Mechanism

Immediate (within minutes): Antigen binds to Fab region of IgE on the surface of mast cell and basophils. This causes adjacent IgE crosslink on the cell surface to crosslink. The mast cell / basophil then degranulates and secretes histamine + tryptase.
Late (within hours): Cytokines recruit inflammatory cells (e.g., eosinophils) → more inflammation.
HY examples are anaphylaxis (i.e., bee sting, peanut allergy), atopy / asthma.
HY examples are post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, polyarteritis nodosa, SLE, arthus reaction, serum sickness.
T cell response (only HS type not associated with antibodies); can be mediated by either CD8+ or CD4+ T cells.
HY examples are PPD skin test for TB, contact dermatitis (poison ivy/oak/sumac, sunscreen, nickel on watches, latex), graft-vs-host disease.

bullets: Antibody production against one’s own cells, tissues, receptors.

bullets: Important point about AR: shows up in peds + causes hepatic fibrosis
Important point about AD: presents in adults; cysts present from birth but just grow + become symptomatic ages 30-40+.
Bacterial meningitis: low glucose, high protein, high neutrophils (polymorphonuclear cells; PMNs)
Aseptic (viral) meningitis: normal glucose, normal (or slightly elevated) protein, high lymphocytes
Fungal meningitis: low glucose, high protein, high lymphocytes (similar to bacterial, but high lymphocytes instead of neutrophils)
1) SABA; then
2) low-dose ICS; then
3) maximize dose ICS; then
That initial order is universal. Then you need to know last resort is oral corticosteroids, however they are most effective. In other words:
After the LABA and before the oral steroids, any number of agents can be given in any order – i.e., nedocromil or cromolyn sodium, zileuton, montelukast, zafirlukast.
Kid + heart tumor = cardiac rhabdomyoma until proven otherwise
Nutrition calorie counts: carbs + protein = 4kcal/g; fat = 9 kcal/g; EtOH = 7kcal/g.
If patient fails the dCCB test, can try agents like bosentan or sildenafil.

Patient has infection + goes into septic shock; Q asks for what LPS binds to that causes shock; answer = Toll-like receptors; in endotoxic shock, the lipid A of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) binds to CD14 on macrophages (toll-like receptor 4; TLR-4), resulting in macrophages releasing cytokines, namely TNF-a and IL-1. Do not confuse endotoxic shock with toxic shock syndrome caused by S. aureus, where TSST toxin (superantigen) bridges MHC-II and TCR, causing the macrophage to release cytokines; if the Q mentions cotton nasal packing or tampons, choose the MHC-II + TCR combo, not CD14/TLR-4.

57M + asks physician why celecoxib increases risk of adverse cardiovascular events; answer = inhibits platelet prostaglandin synthesis without inhibiting thromboxane synthesis; celecoxib is selective COX2 inhibitor.

27M + infertility + high serum testosterone + low serum LH and FSH; what’s the most likely cause of this patient’s infertility; answer = exogenous testosterone use; testosterone-secreting tumor could also theoretically be an answer, but only the former listed.

Biostats Q asks about what increasing the # of participants in a study would result in; answer = decreased standard error of the mean; SEM = SD / (square root of the # of samples); so if samples increase, then the denominator increases, and SEM decreases. Increasing # of samples will also increase power and decrease beta error (false-negative error).
Q asks which of the following agents is an NMDA receptor antagonist; answer = ketamine; NMDA receptors are a type of glutamate receptor; ketamine is an NMDA glutamate receptor antagonist.
Q asks which of the following will occur as a result of giving bortezomib; answer = decreased activation of CD8+ T cells; bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor that causes decreased MHC I expression.

30M + sensory nerve injury in bar fight; Q asks what’s the rate-limiting step in reestablishing normal sensation in this patient; answer = slow anterograde axonal transport; Wallerian degeneration results in breakdown of axonal skeleton and myelin sheath distal to site of nerve injury; nerve regrows anterograde from site of lesion at 1mm/day; slow anterograde transport / regeneration of nerve becomes rate-limiting factor in restoration of function.

rapidFireQAs.a: must do arthrocentesis to rule out septic arthritis

Inheritance pattern of vWD
Heme findings in vWD

rapidFireQAs.a: stabilizes factor VIII in plasma (that’s why aPTT only half time increased)

rapidFireQAs.q: vWD presentation
rapidFireQAs.a: always one platelet problem + one clotting factor problem

Dark urine in SS
Ticlopidine is what?
rapidFireQAs.a: ADP2Y12 blocker anti-platelet agent (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor also)

rapidFireQAs.q: Vomiting a few hours after eating meat
Tx for cerumen buildup
Most common extra-renal location for cysts
Dx of Cryptococcal meningitis?
rapidFireQAs.a: latex agglutination if it’s listed over India ink; mucicarmine staining (red stain) can also be done

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for Cryptococcal meningitis
rapidFireQAs.a: amphotericin B + flucytosine, followed by fluconazole taper

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common immunodeficiency in humans
Motor vehicle accident (MVA) + paradoxical breathing (chest moves outward with exhalation; inward with inhalation)
MVA + rib fractures + underlying infiltrates in lung + low O2 sats
MVA + no rib fractures + non-central chest pain + pulmonary infiltrates underlying the painful area
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary contusion (resources will say “white out of the lung” for pulmonary contusion, but this is buzzywordy and never shows up on actual NBME material)

rapidFireQAs.q: MVA + pulmonary infiltrates + low O2 sats + bolus of normal saline given, resulting in worsening of O2 sats
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary contusion (contused lung is very sensitive to fluid overload)

rapidFireQAs.q: When you get a random ventilator Q and they want an answer
Patient has improving O2 sats on ventilator; next best step?
Crater with necrotic debris on forearm + UC
Biopsy in Crohn
rapidFireQAs.a: non-caseating granulomas; transmural; UC you don’t see these findings

rapidFireQAs.q: Biopsy of DH
Biopsy of small bowel in lactose intolerance
Dx of lactose intolerance
rapidFireQAs.a: hydrogen breath test or decreased stool pH

rapidFireQAs.q: Toxicity of acyclovir
rapidFireQAs.a: nephrotoxicity (crystal nephropathy → acyclovir stones not visible on CT)

rapidFireQAs.q: Don’t give which drugs to patients with HA
What is the product of the t(9;22)
Side-effect of imatinib
Inpatient Tx of MSSA
Tx of MRSA skin infection
rapidFireQAs.a: clindamycin, or TMP/SMX, or doxycycline, or linezolid → vanc has poor skin penetration

rapidFireQAs.q: Suspected incarcerated hernia in a vignette
Most common cause of fever after surgery
Dx of serotonin + carcinoid syndromes
Tx of carcinoid syndrome
12M has ongoing wheezing episodes + is on albuterol inhaler; next best step?
12M has ongoing wheezing episodes + is on albuterol inhaler; what’s most likely to decrease recurrence
rapidFireQAs.a: oral corticosteroids (student says “? I thought you said ICS was what we do next and that oral steroids are last resort” Yeah, you’re right, but they’re still most effective at decreasing recurrence. This isn’t something I’m romanticizing; this distinction is assessed on the FM NBME forms.

rapidFireQAs.q: MOA of nedocromil and cromolyn sodium
MOA of zileuton
rapidFireQAs.a: lipoxygenase inhibitor (enzyme that makes leukotrienes from arachidonic acid)

rapidFireQAs.q: MOA of the -lukasts
rapidFireQAs.a: leukotriene LTC, D, and E4 inhibitors. LTB4 receptor agonism is unrelated and induces neutrophilic chemotaxis (LTB4, IL-8, kallikrein, platelet-activating factor, C5a, bacterial proteins)

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M takes aspirin + gets wheezing; what are we likely to see on physical exam?
Kid has Hx of AERD; physician considers agent to decrease his recurrence of Sx
rapidFireQAs.a: zileuton, or -lukasts (both are correct; and only one will be listed).

rapidFireQAs.q: “Wait, why the low CO2? Aren’t you not able to breathe?”
rapidFireQAs.a: low CO2 is due to high respiratory rate; even if your bronchioles are constricted + filled with secretions, CO2 can diffuse really quickly; in contrast, O2 diffuses slowly and requires healthy airways; that’s why with a high RR, O2 and CO2 are both low (O2 can’t get in, but CO2 can still get out); 19 times out of 20 on the USMLE, if your respiratory rate is high, CO2 is low.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + alcoholic + increased creatine kinase
82F + fell in her house + positive for blood on urine dipstick + negative for RBCs on urine LM
rapidFireQAs.a: rhabdomyolysis (myoglobinuria causes false-positive blood on dipstick)

rapidFireQAs.q: Woman has episiotomy posterior in the midline (vaginal incision made to allow for fetus’s head to pass through birth canal without causing vaginal laceration); if the doctor cuts too far, what will he cut into?
82M + dribbling, hesitancy, interruption of urinary stream + suprapubic mass (bladder) + bacteria in the urine
25F + 6 weeks of dysuria + anterior vaginal wall pain + urinary findings normal
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic interstitial cystitis; must have 6+ weeks of Sx in the absence of any findings; anterior vaginal wall pain sounds weird, but it’s on the obgyn NBME forms, and something to bear in mind is that a cystocele (unrelated) will protrude through the anterior superior vaginal wall, so the anatomic proximity is known to cause symptomatology.

rapidFireQAs.q: Detrusor muscle
rapidFireQAs.a: contracts under parasympathetic activity via the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4); when not voiding, detrusor muscle is kept relaxed by sympathetic activity via the inferior hypogastric nerves (T10-L1).

rapidFireQAs.q: Internal urethral sphincter
rapidFireQAs.a: kept closed by sympathetic activity via inferior hypogastric nerves (T10- L1).

rapidFireQAs.q: External urethral sphincter
rapidFireQAs.a: Opened by somatic activity via the pudendal nerve (S2-4)

rapidFireQAs.q: Need to know low bicarb in pt with dehydration (or any type of shock)
rapidFireQAs.a: lactic acidosis → decreased perfusion to vital organs → decreased oxygen delivery → increased anaerobic respiration → increased lactic acid

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for ethylene glycol and methanol toxicity
rapidFireQAs.a: fomepizole only if listed → in other words, if you get combinations with “ethanol first then fomepizole,” etc., just choose “fomepizole only” if it’s listed

rapidFireQAs.q: Paint thinner + blurry vision
rapidFireQAs.a: methanol toxicity (on one of the later Step 1 NBMEs)

rapidFireQAs.q: How is copper normally excreted by the body?
rapidFireQAs.a: through bile; defective excretory pump in Wilson

rapidFireQAs.q: Pink line tracking up the arm from the palm in 35M who burned himself recently; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: lymphangitis → sporotrichosis is wrong answer (can cause lymphatogenous spread)

rapidFireQAs.q: Brown recluse spider bite
Suspected skin cancer in non-cosmetically sensitive area
Suspected skin cancer on face
rapidFireQAs.a: Mohs surgery (thin slices looking for positive margins)

rapidFireQAs.q: Suspected skin cancer on neck
Most common blood transfusion reaction?
Tx for febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction
rapidFireQAs.a: acetaminophen on the NBME, not prednisone

rapidFireQAs.q: What causes febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction?
rapidFireQAs.a: Abs against donor MHC antigens on RBCs or cytokines from leukocytes in the donor blood

rapidFireQAs.q: 72F + radical mastectomy 25 years ago + hard, raised purple lesions above the elbow; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: lymphangiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome) → you don’t have to agree that it’s HY, but it’s asked on the NBME → caused by chronic lymphatic insufficiency classically years after radical mastectomy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate + spongy 1-cm red lesion on the chest; Dx?
Strawberry hemangioma Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: don’t treat; will grow slightly then regress spontaneously over a few years

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate + large vascular lesion on the leg + thrombocytopenia; what is the cause of the thrombocytopenia?
rapidFireQAs.a: “platelet sequestration.” I’ve memorized this from the NBMEs → similar to splenomegaly, which can cause thrombocytopenia from sequestration within the red pulp, the implication that the large vascular lesion of KMS is that platelets simply get caught within it.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Cherry red blood/lips”
“Brown blood” or “chocolate blood”
Kid with brown blood and they ask you the mechanism (answers are “upregulation of anti-proteinase 2” or “deficiency of cytochrome reductase B5”)
rapidFireQAs.a: deficiency of cytochrome reductase B5; this is on the USMLE. I’m not with you. And if you Wiki it, you’ll see clear as day that they talk about congenital methemoglobinemia due to deficiency of cytochrome reductase B5.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + violaceous papules in a temporal distrubtion
rapidFireQAs.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome; student says “? I thought that was associated with Port wine stain birthmark.” Yeah, if we take a trip back to kindergarten, but you need to know it can present as cutaneous papules in a trigeminal nerve distribution.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M found unconscious on floor in school bathroom + normal vitals + no eye findings + a little sluggish
rapidFireQAs.a: butane (inhalant) toxicity → caused by “dusters” / inhaling computer cleaner; this is on the USMLE!!!

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for varicose veins
47F has varicose veins + painful palpable cord by the ankle (is the treatment compression stockings or subcutaneous enoxaparin; both are listed)
rapidFireQAs.a: subcutaneous enoxaparin because this is superficial thrombophlebitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for arterial insufficiency
rapidFireQAs.a: exercise regimen first, THEN cilostazol (phosphodiesterase 3 inhibitor)

rapidFireQAs.q: Major side-effects of beta-blockers
rapidFireQAs.a: depression + sexual dysfunction (avoid in these patients)

rapidFireQAs.q: Major side-effect of naproxen
rapidFireQAs.a: fluid retention (edema) due to increased renal retention of sodium.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is naproxen?
rapidFireQAs.a: NSAID that the USMLE is obsessed with for some reason.

rapidFireQAs.q: Why might NSAIDs cause fluid retention / renal retention of sodium?
rapidFireQAs.a: knocking out COX → decreased prostaglandin synthesis → decreased renal afferent arteriolar dilatation → decreased renal blood flow → PCT of kidney compensates for perceived low blood volume by increasing Na reabsorption → water follows sodium → edema.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the four beta-blockers that decrease mortality in heart failure?
rapidFireQAs.a: Metoprolol XR (extended release) + carvedilol + nebivolol + bisoprolol → USMLE will never ask “extended-release”; they’ll just want metoprolol, but cardiologists will spasm out if you say regular metoprolol without specifying extended release; the idea being: we don’t give drugs like propranolol, atenolol, etc., for heart failure because they don’t improve mortality.

rapidFireQAs.q: When do we use atenolol
MOA of baclofen
Tx for TA
rapidFireQAs.a: immediate IV methylprednisolone (IV steroids) to prevent blindness, then do temporal artery biopsy; do not choose biopsy before steroids.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of PR
Oral + genital ulcers
What kind of immunofluorescence on biopsy in PV vs BV?
rapidFireQAs.a: Linear in BV; net-like in PV.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for PV and BV
Hematuria + hemoptysis + “head-itis” (mastoiditis, sinusitis, otitis, nasal septal perforation)
Annoying new name for Wegener
Annoying new name for CS
44M + hematuria + hemopytisis + head-itis
What is polyarteritis nodosa
rapidFireQAs.a: medium-vessel vasculitis characterized by immune complex deposition in vascular walls and fibrinoid necrosis

rapidFireQAs.q: Polyarteritis nodosa is associated with what infection?
What do you see on renal artery angiogram in PN
rapidFireQAs.a: “beads on a string” (similar to fibromuscular dysplasia, although completely unrelated diseases).

rapidFireQAs.q: Which vessels are notably not affected in PN
Tx for PN
17M has mononucleosis; how to best decrease risk of transmission?
rapidFireQAs.a: hand washing (“huh, I thought it was just kissing + sharing cups n stuff.” I agree with you. But the USMLE wants handwashing.

rapidFireQAs.q: Question literally asks you point-blank why a patient is given primaquine
How do you Tx the liver abscess?
Fever + periorbital edema + muscle aches + went to a BBQ; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Trichinella spiralis → this is a classic triad seen in trichinosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: How do you get trichinosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: bear meat (yes, Alaska is still in the United States and people hunt polar bear) or pork (pork nematode, not cestode)

rapidFireQAs.q: What is nematode vs cestode vs trematode?
rapidFireQAs.a: nematode is roundworm; cestode tapeworm; trematodes are flukes.

rapidFireQAs.q: Nematode from pork
What does T. solium cause?
“Swiss cheese appearance” of brain in someone who traveled abroad
Single cystic lesion seen on brain CT in someone who went to Mexico
Tx for cysticersosis / neurocysticercosis
rapidFireQAs.a: praziquantel or albendazole (the USMLE will never give you both and make you choose between them; for anti-helminth drugs questions, the correct answer will be the only anti-helminth drug listed).

rapidFireQAs.q: Which helminth causes visceral larva migrans?
Worm in the eye?
How do you get Loa Loa
Upper lobe nodular density in immunocompromised patient
Dx of Aspergilloma
14F has massive unilateral breast mass + mom is freaking out bc her sister died of breast cancer
rapidFireQAs.a: follow-up in six months → virginal breast hypertrophy is normal during puberty.

rapidFireQAs.q: 15M has unilateral mass behind his nipple +/- tenderness of it
rapidFireQAs.a: reassurance → physiologic gynecomastia of puberty (higher androgens are aromatized to estrogens).

rapidFireQAs.q: Girl is Tanner stage 3; which of the following is true?
rapidFireQAs.a: menarche is imminent → USMLE asks this Q straight up and it’s exceedingly HY and frequent.

rapidFireQAs.q: 17F + really pad period pain + physical exam is normal
rapidFireQAs.a: primary dysmenorrhea = prostaglandin hypersecretion (PGF2alpha) → give NSAIDs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 14M is 3rd centile for height + bone age is less than chronologic age; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: constitutional short stature (he’ll catch up; his growth curve is just shifted to the right).

rapidFireQAs.q: 14M is 3rd centile for height; next best step in Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ask for information about the parents’ height trajectory → if they already say in the stem the parents are average height, answer = do bone age.

rapidFireQAs.q: Adult male is 4 feet tall + head and trunk are large in comparison to limbs; Dx?
Tx for DT
rapidFireQAs.a: long-acting benzo (diazepam or lorazepam or chlordiazepoxide) → USMLE likes chlordiazepoxide.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42M has surgery + two days later in hospital he has restlessness + tactile/visual hallucinations; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: alcoholic hallucinosis → on the same spectrum as DT; Tx with long-acting benzo same as DT.

rapidFireQAs.q: MOA of buspirone
2-year-old boy has writhing movements in his sleep + periventricular nodules seen on MRI of the head; what else would be seen in this pt?
rapidFireQAs.a: renal angiomyolipoma or cardiac rhabdomyoma → Dx = tuberous sclerosis (AD).

rapidFireQAs.q: Adult + heart tumor = cardiac myxoma until proven otherwise (ball-in-valve tumor in the left atrium
rapidFireQAs.a: causes a diastolic rumble that abates when patient is positioned in an unusual way, e.g., on his right side while leaning diagonally).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + pedal + forearm edema after commencing anti-hypertensive agent; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: fluid retention / edema caused by dihydropyridine CCB (e.g., nifedipine) → really HY side-effect of d-CCBs!

rapidFireQAs.q: CNS disturbance due to an electrolyte problem
rapidFireQAs.a: high or low sodium; high calcium

rapidFireQAs.q: Cardiac disturbance (arrhythmia) due to an electrolyte problem
rapidFireQAs.a: high or low potassium or calcium

rapidFireQAs.q: Low calcium or potassium not responding to supplementation
rapidFireQAs.a: check serum magnesium (low Mg can cause low Ca and K refractory to supplementation

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets low Mg
rapidFireQAs.a: alcoholics (dietary deficiency; nothing malabsorptive or magic; they just drink too much and fill up on EtOH bc it’s 7kcal/gram).

rapidFireQAs.q: MOA of bosentan
Which of the following is true in the above 28F?
rapidFireQAs.a: “increased vascular expression of endothelin 1.” → if you know bosentan can treat, then inferring this is easy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M takes a drug + gets nystagmus + bellicosity (wants to fight)
2-year-old boy running + playing with 8-year-old sister + they were holding hands and he fell + now he holds arm pronated by his side; Dx?
Tx for nursemaid’s elbow
rapidFireQAs.a: hyperpronation OR gentle supination (both are correct answers; only one will be listed).

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid falls on outstretched arm + pain over anatomical snuffbox; Dx?
When is figure-of-8-strap the answer?
What part of the clavicle gets fractured easiest?
Tx for cubital tunnel syndrome
Perineal gangrene in 50M diabetic
Neonate + strange hereditary disease + mutation analysis shows homozygous gene deletion; what’s the most likely inheritance pattern?
rapidFireQAs.a: autosomal recessive; some students get caught up by saying, “Wait, we’re supposed to know the inheritance pattern of this weird disease?” No. It’s the fact that they say homozygous deletion, without mentioning that either parent has pathology, that implies the condition is autosomal recessive.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient takes nedocromil for seasonal allergies; what’s the MOA of this drug?
rapidFireQAs.a: blocks release of autacoids from cellular storage; student says ?; mast cell stabilizers like nedocromil and cromolyn sodium prevent the release of histamine, which acts as an autacoid, which means it’s a biologic molecule that acts as a local hormone (i.e., acts near site of synthesis).

rapidFireQAs.q: How many kilocalories in one gram of fat, carbs, protein, and ethanol?
rapidFireQAs.a: 9 kcal/g of fat; 4 for both carbs and protein; 7 for ethanol; USMLE Q will give you some nutrition Q where you have to do math, and it will rely on you knowing this nutritional info to get the Q right.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20F + recurrent Staph infections + deficiency of CD18; what mechanism best explains this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: failure of emigration of phagocytes to inflamed tissues; leukocyte adhesion deficiency is caused by deficiency of LFA-1/CD18 integrin, which is required for diapedesis of leukocytes to sites of infection; result is recurrent infections (often Staph) with absent pus; delayed separation of umbilical cord is often omitted from Qs because it’s too easy of a detail.

rapidFireQAs.q: 54F + treated with anti-platelet agent that prevents platelets from interacting with fibrinogen; what’s the agent?
rapidFireQAs.a: abciximab → monoclonal antibody against glycoproteins IIb/IIIa on platelets; these glycoproteins carry out aggregation and are normally bridged by fibrinogen; abciximab is a fibrinogen analogue; don’t confuse aggregation (platelets to each other) via GpIIb/IIIa with adhesion (platelets to endothelium) mediated by Gp Ib. Eptifibitide and tirofiban are lower yield drugs that also inhibit GpIIb/IIIa; abciximab is HY agent with this MOA; HY drugs that inhibit ADP2Y12 receptor on platelets are clopidogrel and prasugrel; ticagrelor and ticlopidine are lower yield drugs that antagonize ADP2Y12.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + receives phentolamine; what intracellular effect is expected?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ phospholipase C activity; phentolamine is a1 antagonist; a1 is coupled to a G-alpha-q G-protein. Agonism will phospholipase C activity, which will ↑ IP3 and ↑ DAG; therefore antagonism will ↓ phospholipase C activity, ↓ IP3, and ↓ DAG.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + has facial nerve and optic nerve on left damaged in car accident; why does he regenerate facial movement over time but not vision?
rapidFireQAs.a: optic nerve is myelinated by oligodendrocytes; oligodendrocyte-myelinated nerves of CNS have limited regenerative capacity compared to Schwann cell-myelinated nerves of the PNS; facial nerve is myelinated by Schwann cells.

rapidFireQAs.q: Woman gets toxoplasmosis but cats isn’t listed as an answer; where did she get it from?
rapidFireQAs.a: pork; can also be written as just simply “delicatessen meats”; both answers on offline NBMEs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + weight loss + progressive shortness of breath + CXR shows pleural-based mass encasing the lungs; what kind of cells are this patient’s malignant cells derived from?
rapidFireQAs.a: mesothelial cells; mesothelioma will classically present with pleural and/or supradiaphragmatic plaques; if shown a gross specimen, mesothelioma will appear to surround the lungs circumferentially, rather than appearing as an isolated mass.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is the role of IkB in relation to NFkB?
rapidFireQAs.a: “releases NFkB after undergoing phosphorylation”; USMLE also wants you to know that corticosteroids ↓ NFkB signaling in leukocytes.

rapidFireQAs.q: 29M + lancinating/stabbing pain in cheek lasting several seconds + happens spontaneously; Q asks location of problem; answer = pons; unusual answer, since trigeminal neuralgia is a peripheral mechanism, but CN V comes from pons; answer can also be “microvascular compression of CN V”; no acute Tx since the Sx subside so quickly; prophylaxis is carbamazepine.
rapidFireQAs.a: Do not confuse trigeminal neuralgia of the V1 distribution with cluster headache; the latter will occur usually during sleep and will last up to half hour; details such as lacrimation and rhinorrhea are HY but too easy and often omitted from Qs; Q can mention pupillary changes during cluster headache; Tx = 100% oxygen; prophylaxis is verapamil (not propranolol). Migraine prophylaxis on USMLE = propranolol (sometimes just written as beta blockade); Tx is NSAIDs followed by triptans (serotonin receptor agonists).

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + relaxing after coming back from a run; which of the following describes her changes in diastole and systole as her heart rate returns to normal?
rapidFireQAs.a: diastole increases more than systole; the Q can also be asked as the inverse: that is, as HR increases, diastole shortens more than systole; the learning point is that the slower the heart rate, the greater the proportion of time spent in diastole.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + chest pain that does not change with position + chest pain worse with palpation; diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: costochondritis; even though it doesn’t change with position, it worsens with palpation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + found in street with hypothermia + rewarmed in hospital + picture is shown of her feet and they’re red; what electrolyte are we most worried about?
rapidFireQAs.a: hyperkalemia → reperfusion injury causes oxygen radicals that increase the risk of rhabdo, especially in alcoholics.

rapidFireQAs.q: 82F + found in her house by the staircase; urine blood is 2+; RBCs on urine light microscopy are 3-4 per high-power field; diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: rhabdomyolysis; classic finding is false-positive blood on urine dipstick; USMLE can give 3-4 RBCs/hpf as false-positive.

rapidFireQAs.q: Question gives 40s male with duodenal ulcers caused by H. pylori. Following antibiotic treatment, they ask what lifestyle variable is most likely to promote healing of ulcers
rapidFireQAs.a: smoking cessation. Reducing alcohol intake can also help, but I’ve seen smoking cessation as answer on NBME, where they don’t have abstinence from alcohol as an answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: 11F + rhinoconjunctivitis past month; Q asks what to ask parents about
rapidFireQAs.a: “recent pets in household”; if recent allergy-like presentation in a patient with no prior Hx, inquire about pets.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + diabetic + high LDL + low HDL + high BMI; Q asks best way to decrease long-term complications in this patient
rapidFireQAs.a: “good glycemic control”; generic answer, similar to smoking cessation, but this is HY.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + long history of alcoholism and smoking + pulsatile mass in epigastrium; Q wants to know #1 way to have prevented this patient’s condition → answer = smoking cessation; the demographic that classically gets AAA is: elderly males who are ever-smokers; alcohol is not salient risk factor; diabetes is actually slightly protective of AAA due to the stiffening effect of glycosylation on endothelium.
rapidFireQAs.a: Guidelines vary on screening for AAA, but updated literature says both men and women 65- 75 who have ever-smoked should get a one-off abdominal ultrasound to screen for AAA. Lower thresholds can be used in patients with family history.

rapidFireQAs.q: 14M + hits head while skateboarding + loses consciousness briefly + head CT shows biconvex-shaped bleed; what is major risk factor
rapidFireQAs.a: head temporal trauma resulting in rupture of middle meningeal artery.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + has diabetic foot ulcer; Q asks how this condition could have best been prevented
rapidFireQAs.a: wearing comfortable-fitting shoes; wrong answer is nightly foot checks. Both are important to prevent foot ulcers, but if both choices are listed together, choose wearing comfortable-fitting shoes.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + long-standing diabetes + diarrhea; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: diabetic neuropathy to bowel affecting hypogastric nerves (loss of anti-peristalsis sympathetic nerves → causes too much peristalsis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + long-standing diabetes + constipation; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: diabetic neuropathy to bowel affecting pelvic splanchnic nerves (loss of pro-peristalsis parasympathetic nerves).

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + painful thyroid + low uptake of radioiodine on scan; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (aka deQuervain); risk factor is viral infection; answer on USMLE for tender/painful thyroid.

rapidFireQAs.q: 60M + had gastrectomy performed 6 months ago + now has neuropathy; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: B12 deficiency due to gastrectomy (loss of parietal cells which produce intrinsic factor).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + vegan + high MCV + hyper-segmented neutrophil on smear; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: B12 deficiency due to veganism (can also be strict vegetarianism).

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + giving birth + fetal anterior shoulder caught behind mother’s pubic symphysis; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: shoulder dystocia; risk factor is fetal macrosomia due to maternal diabetes (causes big baby). This can cause clavicular fracture in the newborn.

rapidFireQAs.q: Above 34F + experiences excessive vaginal bleeding despite McRobert’s maneuver to deliver in setting of shoulder dystocia; Dx + risk factor? → vaginal laceration due to macrosomia from maternal diabetes.
rapidFireQAs.a: In short: maternal diabetes causes fetal macrosomia → results in shoulder dystocia → results in fetal clavicular fracture + maternal vaginal laceration during delivery.

rapidFireQAs.q: 30F + 38 weeks’ gestation + fever 103F + CVA tenderness; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: pyelonephritis; uterus can compress ureters in third trimester, increasing risk for pyelo; in addition, progesterone slows ureteral peristalsis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + pregnant + abnormal AFP measurement; risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: dating error is most common cause of abnormal AFP measurement; next best step is fetal ultrasound to get correct dates (i.e., crown-rump length); re-measure AFP is wrong answer (the lab result wasn’t wrong, just the ultrasound date estimate was).

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + pregnant + low AFP + low estriol + high b-hCG + high inhibin A; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: Down syndrome due to increased maternal age.

rapidFireQAs.q: 4M + recent gastroenteritis + now has diarrhea after meals; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: lactose intolerance; risk factor is recent GI viral infection; the latter can cause transient lactose intolerance due to sloughing of brush border (hence losing disaccharidase).

rapidFireQAs.q: 4M + small, shrunken kidney + tubular atrophy seen on biopsy; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic pyelonephritis; major risk factor is recurrent acute pyelo, either from vesicoureteral reflux or posterior urethral valves (can be written on NBME as “congenital urethral obstruction”).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + various medium-sized arteries with fibrinoid necrosis and segmental, beaded, “rosary sign”; diagnosis + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: polyarteritis nodosa; major risk factor is hepatitis B (30% of patients with PA are seropositive for HepB).
